newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: S.E. Asia currencies lack verve after Thai plan.
newsitem.headline: S.E. Asia currencies lack verve after Thai plan.

text.p: Southeast Asian currencies traded listlessly on Wednesday as the market held out for more specifics from Thailand's economic rescue package.

The eagerly awaited plan -- a series of tough measures aimed at cutting the current account deficit and reviving Thailand's beleaguered economy -- was applauded by Japan and Washington, but dealers said it was an anti-climax to the market.
The Thai baht firmed slightly after Finance Minister Thanong Bidaya said Thailand would lift the two-tier baht system imposed in mid-May to counter speculative attacks on the currency.
But he gave no date and dealers said the baht hit a barrier around the 30.80 to the dollar level in offshore markets.
The Thai unit was at 31.60/70 to the dollar onshore at 0930 GMT, little changed from its midday levels. It was at 30.80/31.00 offshore against 31.05/15 earlier.

"There are a lot of hopeful people in the market. Everyone knows they have to lift it eventually because it's hurting them more than it's hurting us. But the question is when and how," a Singapore-based dealer said.
Chia Woon Khien, head of Asian research at Skandinaviska Enskilda Banken, said there was unlikely to be an immediate impact from lifting the controls.
"The rates have already converged between onshore and offshore so there isn't a gap that needs to be closed," she said.
"But the fact that they are going to lift it would mean the baht is opening up its defence. And there's a danger that if the IMF package doesn't work out well, there could be a problem."
Malaysia's ringgit recouped some of early losses on dollar sales by exporters but dealers said it was likely to remain under pressure in the near future.
They said players had largely discounted news of central bank curbs on currency swap transactions and dealers said the ringgit could test recent lows.
"The dollar trend is still strong. The swaps restriction will not be effective for a while as the market is well funded," said a dealer with a European bank in Singapore.
The ringgit was at 2.6355/85 to the dollar against 2.6400/30 at midday.

Bank Negara ordered local banks to limit non-trade related currency swaps to $2.0 million with each overseas customer from Monday, as part of an effort to cool speculation in the ringgit and bring down interest rates.
The Singapore dollar was little moved, remaining between 1.4690-1.4750 to the U.S. dollar all day.
The Indonesian rupiah continued to look firm amid tight money market liquidity and lingering fears Bank Indonesia might impose curbs similar to those in Malaysia.
"Sentiment on the rupiah seems to have improved. We even see some 'good name' foreign investors looking for rupiah assets to lock in current attractive rates," a state bank dealer in Jakarta said.
But dealers said the rupiah's gains were likely to be limited to 2,580 for the time being.

The Philippine peso ended stronger at 28.45/55 to the dollar against Tuesday's 28.65 close. Manila traders said banks sold dollars to abide by the central bank's newly imposed five percent limit on long dollar positions.
The Philippine central bank dropped its overnight borrowing rate to 18 percent from 20 percent with effect from Thursday. It also cut the overnight lending rate to 22 from 25 percent.
The Taiwan dollar ended lower despite early central bank support which took it to an intra-day high of T$28.550.
Dealers said waves of dollar purchases emerged to pull the Taiwan dollar down late in the day. It ended at T$28.656 against Tuesday's T$28.625 finish.
